chapter: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
title: Rivalry with young pianist John Roland Redd of Red Perkins' band
summary: A teenage pianist related to bandleader Red Perkins, later a Hollywood TV organist, was Thompson's friendly competitor and co-winner of an amateur contest.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: But I had heard pianists like that, and I was very highly inspired by playing the piano then. Not only that but I had some competition in that particular city. There was an orchestra there who later on I found out came from Omaha, Nebraska, where I later played with my first large band of importance. But at this time there was an orchestra by the name of Red -- I can't think of his last name. Isn't that something?
Was he also a high school student?
No, this was a man.
Oh.

But there was a student who was younger than I. I was I think 16, he was 12, something like that, or 14, and he played terrific piano. This young boy, he could play like Claude Hawkins, he could play like almost anybody. His name was John Rhona Dred. The name of the band was Red Perkins, P-e-r-k-i-n-s.
Right.
Red Perkins. Yes, very, very fine entertaining, musical orchestra. And this John Rhona Dred was some relation to him, cousin or something.
How do you spell John Rhona Dred?
John Rollin, like Rollin CerK.
I see.
R-o-l-l-i-n. I think two /l/s.
Yes, that's right.
John, that was his middle name, and for some reason or other used all three names.
Yes.
And he later on went to Hollywood and became a famous organist, and I believe he used another name under some Turkish title.
Oh.

And became rather famous as one of the first TV organists who was featured in the Hollywood area. This was early in the early forties, somewhere along in there, like about '40, '41, something like that. But any way this was like a competition for me, which, you know, competition makes you either give up or makes you better.
Stirs you on.

Yes. So this was enough competition to really inspire me to have something to shoot at, you know, as a challenge. And most musical challenges are very friendly type you might say, they're not like two guys in a ring, you know.
Yeah.
But you have some pride and you want to be as good as the other fella, at least, you know, if not
better. And we live primarily you might say by the applause, and the acclaim.
Yes.
And so this really gave me this fire necessary to really try to play more -- play the piano, you know. And we were like controversial boy piano players.
Yes.

And the fact of the matter is we won an amateur contest together in one of the local theatres. The irony of this particular story also is it was hardly able to tell which one of us was oldest because I was -- he and I were about the same size. He was about 12 or 14, I was 16. So no one really knew.
No.

But I really think he was a much better, experienced piano player than I was because he had a better background than I. And then he had the experience of playing with his uncle's band on the road, you see, so he had much more experience than I did.
But he didn't the pull that you had in the other direction. You had to divide your interests for a while, didn't you?
Oh, yes, yes, of course.
You know, I mean you had a classical background in your home, and he probably didn't. Who was the
winner of this contest?

Well, first I'd like to correct you. I believe he did have a classical background, in fact he might have had even more a formal classical background than I did, although I don't know for sure. All I know is that he was very proficient at playing the piano, and he could play -- he had been tutored quite well by his relatives. Naturally as I said there's quite a bit of difference when you have a relative who is a band leader. You have this firsthand information. And as I said, the experience of playing in public.
